workedExamples.stem:
Hydrogen reacts with chlorine: $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$. Use the bond energies in the table.
(a) Calculate the energy taken in to break the bonds in the reactants. [1]
(b) Calculate the energy given out when the bonds in the products are made. [1]
(c) Calculate the energy change for the reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic. [2]

data.caption: Bond energies for the reaction between hydrogen and chlorine.

steps.working: Bonds broken: one H–H and one Cl–Cl. 436 + 242 = 678 kJ.
steps.decision: Read the formulae, not the table: H₂ has one H–H bond and Cl₂ one Cl–Cl bond, so each energy is counted once here.

steps.working: Bonds made: two molecules of HCl, each with one H–Cl bond. 2 × 431 = 862 kJ.
steps.decision: The 2 in front of HCl means two molecules, so the H–Cl energy is counted twice. Counting it once gives 431 kJ and the answer that follows is wrong.

options: Because the balancing number tells you how many molecules there are
Because H–Cl bonds are twice as strong as the others
Because there are two different elements in HCl
whyMenu.explain: The big number in front multiplies everything in that formula, bonds included.

steps.working: Energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 678 − 862 = -184 kJ.
steps.decision: Broken first, made second. Doing it the other way round gives 184 kJ — the right size with the wrong sign, which reverses the chemistry.

steps.working: The energy change is negative, so the reaction is exothermic.
steps.decision: Write the minus sign on the answer line. Summer 2023's report records candidates being reminded that the negative sign is needed for full credit.

accepted: The energy change is negative, so the reaction is exothermic.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 678 kJ. (b) 862 kJ. (c) 678 − 862 = -184 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

steps.working: The products go above the reactants, because the reaction has taken energy in.
steps.decision: Decide the product level before you draw anything else. Endothermic finishes higher; exothermic finishes lower. Getting this wrong loses the mark that every other mark sits on.

steps.working: One smooth line from the reactant level, up over a hump, down to the product level.
steps.decision: One line only, and keep the whole of it above the horizontal axis. The 2024 report names two lines and a product line below the axis as errors to avoid.

steps.working: A: a single-headed arrow from the reactant level up to the top of the hump.
steps.decision: The activation energy is the climb from where the reactants start, not from the product level and not the whole height of the graph.

steps.working: E: a single-headed arrow between the reactant level and the product level.
steps.decision: The energy change is the gap between the two levels. Use single-headed arrows: the report asks for them by name.

steps.working: The activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.
steps.decision: The glossary wording. It is a threshold before the reaction, never the energy the reaction gives out.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Products drawn above reactants, joined by one smooth curve over a hump. (b) A from the reactant level to the top of the hump; E between the reactant and product levels. (c) The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur.

items.stem: A thermometer reads 21.0 °C, then 27.5 °C. What has happened to the temperature?
items.skill: Prerequisite from mathematics — reading a change; you are not expected to have met energy changes yet

options.text: it has risen by 6.5 °C
options.feedback: Finish minus start. Every experiment in this lesson comes down to that subtraction.

options.text: it has fallen by 6.5 °C
options.feedback: 27.5 is the larger number, so the temperature has gone up. Which way it goes is the whole point of the topic.

options.text: it has risen by -6.5 °C
options.feedback: That is start minus finish, which gives a negative rise. Take the starting temperature away from the final one.

items.stem: In the formula 2HCl, what does the 2 in front tell you?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.5 — reading a balanced equation

options.text: there are two molecules of HCl
options.feedback: A number in front multiplies the whole formula. Section 4 uses this to count bonds.

options.text: there are two hydrogen atoms in the molecule
options.feedback: That would be written H₂, with the 2 as a subscript after the H. A number in front counts whole molecules.

options.text: the bond is twice as strong
options.feedback: The number says how many molecules there are; it tells you nothing about bond strength.

options.text: a force holding two atoms together
options.feedback: Holding them together, which is why pulling them apart takes energy. That single fact runs through the whole of section 4.

options.text: the gap between two atoms
options.feedback: A bond is a force of attraction, not a space. Because it holds the atoms together, breaking it needs energy put in.

options.text: a store of heat inside a molecule
options.feedback: Not a store you can tip out: energy has to be supplied to break a bond, and is released when one forms.

items.stem: A reaction is carried out in a polystyrene cup and the temperature falls. What kind of reaction is it?

options.text: endothermic, because heat has been taken in
options.feedback: The mixture has taken heat from its surroundings, so the surroundings — and the thermometer — cool down.

options.text: exothermic, because heat has been taken in
options.feedback: Exothermic means heat is given OUT, and the temperature would rise. The two halves of this answer do not go together.

options.text: exothermic, because heat has been given out
options.feedback: Heat given out would warm the mixture and the temperature would rise. Here it fell.

options.text: neither, because the temperature only fell a little
options.feedback: Any measurable fall means heat has been taken in. The size of the change does not decide which word applies.

items.stem: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, where is the product level drawn?

options.text: below the reactant level
options.feedback: Energy has left the chemicals, so they finish lower than they started.

options.text: above the reactant level
options.feedback: That is the endothermic profile. Exothermic finishes lower, because energy has been given out.

options.text: at the same level as the reactants
options.feedback: Level ends would mean no energy change at all, and then the reaction would be neither exothermic nor endothermic.

options.text: at the top of the hump
options.feedback: The top of the hump is the peak the reaction passes through, not where it finishes.

items.stem: Which statement about bonds is correct?

options.text: breaking bonds takes energy in; making bonds gives energy out
options.feedback: In to break, out to make. Every bond-energy calculation is built on that one line.

options.text: breaking bonds gives energy out; making bonds takes energy in
options.feedback: The exact swap Summer 2023 examiners reported. A bond holds atoms together, so pulling them apart has to be paid for.

options.text: both breaking and making bonds take energy in
options.feedback: If both took energy in, no reaction could ever give out heat. Making a bond releases energy.

options.text: neither breaking nor making bonds involves energy
options.feedback: Both do, and the balance between them is exactly what decides whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

items.stem: For $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$, the bonds broken total 678 kJ and the bonds made total 862 kJ. What is the energy change?

options.feedback: Bonds broken − bonds made = 678 − 862 = -184 kJ, and the negative sign says exothermic.

options.text: 184 kJ
options.feedback: That is bonds made minus bonds broken. The right size, but the sign now says the reaction takes heat in, which is the opposite of the truth.
The two totals are subtracted, not added: one is energy going in and the other energy coming out.

options.text: 247 kJ
options.feedback: That counts only one H–Cl bond. Two molecules of HCl form, so the H–Cl energy is counted twice.

items.stem: An energy change works out as a negative number. What does that mean?

options.text: more energy was given out than taken in, so the reaction is exothermic
options.feedback: Negative means exothermic, and the sign is part of the answer: leaving it off loses the mark.

options.text: more energy was taken in than given out, so the reaction is endothermic
options.feedback: That is what a positive answer means. Negative says the products hold less energy than the reactants.

options.text: a mistake has been made, because energy cannot be negative
options.feedback: The minus sign shows the direction the energy travelled, not a negative amount of energy.

options.text: the reaction does not happen
options.feedback: Most reactions you meet have a negative energy change. It tells you the reaction gives out heat, not that it fails.

options.text: the minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
options.feedback: A threshold on the way in, drawn as the height of the hump above the reactant level.

options.text: the energy given out by the reaction
options.feedback: That is the energy change, measured between the two levels. The activation energy is the climb before it.

options.text: the difference between the reactant and product levels
options.feedback: That gap is the energy change. The activation energy runs from the reactant level to the top of the hump.

options.text: the energy stored in the products
options.feedback: A profile shows energy differences, not absolute stores, and the activation energy is a difference on the way in.

parts.stem:
Hydrogen reacts with chlorine: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.

hints: How many molecules of HCl are made?

parts.stem: Calculate the energy change for the reaction. Give your answer in kJ.

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2023 C2 Higher: candidates must include the negative sign to gain full credit.

hints: Bonds broken first, bonds made second.
The sign is part of the answer.
parts.workedSolution: Energy change = bonds broken − bonds made = 678 − 862 = -184 kJ.

commonErrors.feedback: That is bonds made minus bonds broken, which turns the sign round and says the reaction takes heat in. Broken first, made second.

indicativeContent.point: Bonds in the reactants must be broken, and breaking bonds takes energy in.
Bonds in the products are made, and making bonds gives energy out.
More energy is given out making bonds than is taken in breaking them.
So the energy change is negative and the reaction is exothermic.
Carry out the reaction in a polystyrene cup with a lid, to reduce heat loss.
Record the starting temperature and the highest temperature reached with a thermometer.
A rise in temperature shows that heat has been given out to the surroundings.

scheme.for: a banded answer covering both halves: bonds broken take energy in, bonds made give energy out, more out than in so the change is negative and the reaction exothermic; and a method using an insulated cup with a lid, a thermometer, a starting reading and a highest reading, with the rise as the evidence
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Two halves: the bonds, and the measurement.
Say what you would record, and what the reading would show.
parts.workedSolution: Before the reaction can happen the bonds in the hydrogen and chlorine molecules have to be broken, and breaking bonds takes energy in. New bonds are then made in the hydrogen chloride, and making bonds gives energy out. More energy is given out making the new bonds than was taken in breaking the old ones, so the energy change is negative and the reaction is exothermic. To show this, carry the reaction out in a polystyrene cup with a lid, which reduces heat loss to the room. Record the starting temperature with a thermometer, then the highest temperature reached. A rise in temperature shows that heat has been given out to the surroundings.

findTheMistake.stem:
Fiachra is asked: 'Use the bond energies H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242 and H–Cl 431 kJ to find the energy change for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, and say whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. [3]'
His working:
studentWorking: Energy change = 862 − 678 = 184 kJ, so the reaction is endothermic
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Both totals are right. The subtraction is the wrong way round: the rule is bonds broken minus bonds made. Doing it the other way gives the right size with the wrong sign, and the sign is what decides exothermic from endothermic — so the conclusion flips too.
correction: Energy change = 678 − 862 = -184 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: both totals stand and they carry forward. Write the rule out before you subtract — energy change = bonds broken − bonds made — and the sign takes care of itself. Summer 2024 examiners record missing and reversed signs as a common error on this question.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'Hydrogen burns in oxygen: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Use the bond energies H–H 436 kJ, O=O 498 kJ and O–H 464 kJ to calculate the energy change, and say whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. [3]'
Her working:
studentWorking: Energy change = 1370 − 928 = +442 kJ, so the reaction is endothermic
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Each water molecule has two O–H bonds, and the 2 in front of H₂O makes two molecules: four O–H bonds are made, not two. Her bonds-made total is half what it should be, so the subtraction comes out positive and her conclusion flips. Her line 1 is right, and her line 3 follows correctly from line 2.
correction: Energy change = 1370 − 1856 = −486 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: bonds broken is right, and her subtraction is carried through correctly from her own total (error carried forward). Count the bonds in one molecule, then multiply by the big number in front. The Summer 2024 report names miscalculated product totals as a common error on this question.

prompts.answer: Breaking a bond takes energy in; making a bond gives energy out.

prompts.prompt: Write the rule for the energy change of a reaction from bond energies.
prompts.answer: Energy change = energy taken in to break bonds − energy given out when bonds are made.

prompts.prompt: Your bond-energy answer comes out negative. What does that mean, and what must you not leave off?
prompts.answer: Negative means more energy was given out than taken in, so the reaction is exothermic. The minus sign must be written on the answer line.

prompts.prompt: Which way does the energy change arrow point for an exothermic reaction?
prompts.answer: Down, from the reactant level to the lower product level.

prompts.prompt: A reaction runs backwards. What happens to the size and sign of its energy change?
prompts.answer: The size stays the same; the sign is reversed.
